title: Energy Landscape — Attractors in Bipolar Disorder
subtitle: Click drugs to toggle. You can combine many. Observe onset and decay.

attractorTheory.title: Attractor Theory of Bipolar Disorder
attractorTheory.description: Bipolar disorder can be understood as a disease of the brain's 'energy landscape'. In this model, states like Mania and Depression are stable 'basins' (attractors) that the system naturally falls into. Without treatment, Euthymia (stable mood) is often an unstable peak — like a ball balanced on a hill — where any stressor can easily push the system into a pathological state. Medications like Lithium work by reshaping this landscape, making euthymia a stable attractor.
attractorTheory.link: Read more: 'A dynamic energy landscape of the genome organization in bipolar disorder' (Nature, 2022)

lithium.label: Lithium
lithium.desc: The ONLY drug that reshapes the entire landscape. Euthymia becomes a deep, stable well. Other drugs only fill wells or slow the ball.
lithium.detail: The oldest and best-documented stabilizer. The only one with strong neuroprotective effects and significant suicide risk reduction.

sections.heading: Proven mechanisms
items: Inositol pathway — inhibits IMPase, limiting excessive signaling in overactive neurons
GSK-3beta blockade — stabilizes synaptic plasticity and circadian rhythms
Neuroprotection — increases BDNF, reverses gray matter loss in hippocampus and prefrontal cortex
Glutamate/GABA modulation — shifts the balance towards inhibition
Mitochondria — improves cellular respiration and reduces oxidative stress

sections.heading: Key clinical facts
items: Reduces relapse risk by ~40% vs placebo
The only psychiatric drug significantly lowering suicide risk
Reverses brain volume loss associated with the disease

sections.heading: Systemic hypothesis
items: Bipolarity is a disease of attractor dynamics — the brain has too deep, unstable basins (mania/depression) and a flattened center (euthymia)
Lithium doesn't target one receptor — it reduces 'gain' in feedback loops across many levels simultaneously
Acts as a network noise reducer — stabilizes mitochondrial metabolism in network nodes
Restores metabolic flexibility — widens the stability range of the glycolytic (mania) to oxidative (depression) switch
Dynamic models confirm: lithium changes energy landscape topology, not just individual signal strength

valproate.label: Valproate
valproate.desc: The ball moves through 'honey' — transitions between states are slower, but the landscape remains the same.
valproate.detail: Enhances GABAergic transmission and blocks voltage-gated sodium channels. Effective mainly in acute mania and rapid cycling. Terrain (wells) remains unchanged — the drug slows ball dynamics.

lamotrigine.label: Lamotrigine
lamotrigine.desc: Shallows the depressive well (glutamate blockade) — but mania remains deep. Asymmetric protection.
lamotrigine.detail: Blocks voltage-gated sodium channels and inhibits glutamate release. Well-documented efficacy in preventing depressive episodes. Requires slow dose titration.

aripiprazole.label: Aripiprazole
aripiprazole.desc: Shallows the manic well and sets a moderate barrier ('D2 thermostat'). If the ball is in mania, it gradually flows out.
aripiprazole.detail: Acts as a partial D2 agonist and 5-HT2A antagonist. 'Modulates' dopamine rather than blocking it completely. Prevents manic relapse.

quetiapine.label: Quetiapine
quetiapine.desc: Shallows both wells (mania and depression) + sedation + barrier. Bidirectional, but metabolically heavy.
quetiapine.detail: Broad receptor profile (D2, 5-HT2A, H1). Effective in both mania AND bipolar depression (BOLDER studies). Low gravity represents sedation.

olanzapine.label: Olanzapine
olanzapine.desc: Strongest shallowing of the manic well — ball is pushed out even from deep mania. Strong sedation.
olanzapine.detail: High affinity for D2, 5-HT2A, H1 and muscarinic receptors. One of the most effective drugs for acute mania. High metabolic risk.

risperidone.label: Risperidone
risperidone.desc: Significant shallowing of mania + barrier. Rapid effect, but risk of stiffness.
risperidone.detail: Potent D2 antagonist. Rapidly reduces manic agitation. Risk of extrapyramidal symptoms.

clonazepam.label: Clonazepam
clonazepam.desc: Floods the landscape with oil (massive GABA). Rapid relief, no structural repair — 'rebound' after withdrawal.
clonazepam.detail: Benzodiazepine. Potent slowing (damping) but no effect on well depth. Risk of tolerance and dependence.

thc.label: THC
thc.desc: Dysregulates the landscape — wells oscillate randomly. Temporary relief but higher risk of episodes over time.
thc.detail: Disrupts neurotransmitter regulation. Jitter in visualization represents mood instability.

ketamine.label: Ketamine
ketamine.desc: Instantly fills the depressive well (NMDA blockade). Spectacular but short-lived effect.
ketamine.detail: Rapid antidepressant effect via NMDA blockade and synaptogenesis. Does not permanently change topology.

mdma.label: MDMA
mdma.desc: Shallows both wells (massive 5-HT/DA) + high chaos. Mania risk.
mdma.detail: Massive monoamine release. High risk in bipolar — may trigger mania or worsen depression (crash).

ect.label: ECT
ect.desc: Landscape reset — mania and depression become almost flat, euthymia becomes a true attractor.
ect.detail: Electroconvulsive therapy. Most potent method for breaking severe episodes. Dramatic topological change.

alcohol.label: Alcohol
alcohol.desc: Destabilizes the landscape by deepening both pathological basins. Temporary slowing gives way to increased chaos and relapse risk.
alcohol.detail: CNS depressant (GABAergic). While initially slowing the ball (sedation), its long-term effects and rebound deepen both manic and depressive wells, making them stronger attractors. Increases cycling and impulsivity.
